warmup.q: A team says: "We'll put GraphQL in front of our services, so we get a graph database for free." A client asks for 50 payments, each with its account. With one resolver per field and no batching, how many calls reach the accounts service?
options: One: GraphQL joins the data inside the database
50: the account resolver runs once per payment
None: GraphQL caches every account it has seen
Two: one per level of the query
warmup.why: GraphQL is a query language for APIs, not a database. The server runs a resolver for each field of each object, so the account resolver runs once per payment: 50 calls, plus one for the list. That's the N+1 problem from the SQL track's JDBC lesson, one layer up. One call per level is what batching gets you, and it isn't the default.

sections.h: A triple is the smallest record there is: subject, predicate, object
sections.html:
Lesson 8 stored a graph as nodes and relationships, each with properties. Strip that down as far as it goes and every fact becomes three strings: M-0042 name "Northwind Bikes", C-7 owns M-0042, C-2 owns C-7. The first part is the subject, the second the predicate, the third the object. When the object is a plain value, the triple is a property. When it names another thing, the triple is an edge. That's the whole data model of RDF, the Resource Description Framework, and a database that stores it is a triple store. The figure shows five triples as a table and as a graph.

@prefix ex: <https://example.test/pay#> .

ex:M-0042  ex:name     "Northwind Bikes" .
ex:C-7     ex:owns     ex:M-0042 .
ex:C-2     ex:owns     ex:C-7 ;
           ex:country  "LU" .

That's Turtle, the most readable of RDF's text formats. Names are IRIs, web-style global identifiers, shortened here with the prefix ex:. Global names are RDF's real idea. Two datasets that both say https://example.test/pay#C-7 mean the same company, so you merge them by putting the triples in one store. Merging two relational databases needs both sides to agree on a schema first.

A SPARQL query, RDF's query language, is a set of triple patterns: triples with variables in some positions. "Who owns a company that owns M-0042, and where is it registered?" is

SELECT ?owner ?country WHERE {
    ?owner  ex:owns     ?mid .
    ?mid    ex:owns     ex:M-0042 .
    ?owner  ex:country  ?country .
}

Each pattern matches triples, and a variable used twice must take the same value both times. So the first two patterns join on ?mid and the third joins on ?owner. A SPARQL query is a join of one three-column table with itself, once per pattern. That's the picture for this lesson, and the next two sections are two more ways to ask a graph for things. A property path says "one or more hops" directly: ?c ex:owns+ ex:M-0042 finds every company above M-0042 at any depth, lesson 7's recursive CTE in one line.

Where does RDF stand in 2026? The Semantic Web it was built for never arrived, but the model lives on. Wikidata publishes its knowledge graph as RDF and answers SPARQL, the schema.org markup in web pages is often JSON-LD, which is RDF written as JSON, and Amazon Neptune serves SPARQL next to property graphs. The standards move slowly. RDF 1.2 Concepts and RDF 1.2 Semantics became W3C Candidate Recommendations on 7 April 2026. They add triple terms, a triple used as the object of another triple, so the store can say who reported an ownership and when. SPARQL 1.2 was still a Working Draft in mid-2026.

try.title: Turn a row into triples, and a question into patterns
steps: Take one row of the payments table: payment_id = 'pay-81723', account_id = 'A-1001', merchant_id = 'M-0042', amount_minor = 4250. Write it as triples with ex:pay-81723 as the subject, one triple per other column.
Write the SPARQL triple patterns for "every merchant account A-1001 paid, with the merchant's name". Which variable joins which patterns?
Predict: if A-1001 paid M-0042 twice, how many rows come back, and what changes it to one?
try.expect:
ex:pay-81723  ex:account      ex:A-1001 .
ex:pay-81723  ex:merchant     ex:M-0042 .
ex:pay-81723  ex:amountMinor  4250 .

SELECT ?m ?name WHERE {
    ?p  ex:account   ex:A-1001 .
    ?p  ex:merchant  ?m .
    ?m  ex:name      ?name .
}

One row with three non-key columns is three triples, which is why triple stores count billions of triples for millions of things. ?p joins the first two patterns and ?m joins the second and third. Two payments to M-0042 give two bindings of ?p, so two rows with the same merchant; SELECT DISTINCT ?m ?name returns one, as DISTINCT does in SQL.

sections.h: Datalog defines a relation with rules, and a rule may name itself
sections.html:
Triple patterns answer questions of a fixed shape. "Every company above M-0042, at any depth" needs a definition that refers to itself. Datalog, a database language from 1980s research and a subset of Prolog, is built for exactly that. A program has facts, which are rows, and rules, which define new relations from old ones, the way a view does:

owns("C-7", "M-0042").    owns("C-2", "C-7").    owns("C-9", "C-7").

controls(X, Y) :- owns(X, Y).
controls(X, Z) :- controls(X, Y), owns(Y, Z).

Read :- as "if" and the comma as "and"; capitalized names are variables. X controls Y if X owns Y. X controls Z if X controls some Y and Y owns Z. The second rule names controls on both sides, so it's recursive, and the shared variable Y is a join, like a shared ?mid in SPARQL. The program has no loop and no stop condition. The engine applies the rules round after round until a round derives nothing new, a state called the fixpoint.

The simplest engine, naive evaluation, re-applies every rule to everything known so far. Count its work on a chain of 200 companies, C-1 owns C-2 owns ... owns C-200. At the end there are 19,900 controls facts, one per pair. Naive evaluation needs 199 rounds, and because round 150 re-joins every fact rounds 1 to 149 already found, it makes about 2.6 million derivations to keep 19,900. Double the chain and the work goes up eight times; the Try-it shows the curve.

Semi-naive evaluation fixes that with one observation: a new fact needs a new ingredient. If neither controls(X, Y) nor owns(Y, Z) changed since the last round, joining them again can only rediscover old facts. So each round joins only the delta, the facts that were new in the previous round. On the same chain that's 19,900 derivations, each fact exactly once, in the same 199 rounds. You've met it already: PostgreSQL's working table from lesson 7, where the recursive term sees only the previous round's rows, is semi-naive evaluation. The stepper runs it on four companies.

Datalog is a niche database and a busy tool. Datomic, which Nubank made free in 2023, answers queries in Datalog over datoms: a triple plus a transaction id and an added-or-retracted flag. Soufflé compiles Datalog to parallel C++ for static program analysis; its latest release is 2.5, from March 2025. GitHub's CodeQL finds security bugs with QL, and the QL docs say its semantics are based on Datalog, recursive predicates included. Google's open-source Mangle extends Datalog with aggregation, as a Go library.

try.title: Watch naive evaluation's work grow
steps: Read NaiveRoundsDemo.kt. It runs naive evaluation of the two controls rules on ownership chains of 50, 100, 200 and 400 companies and counts the rounds and the derivations.
Before you run it: how many facts does a chain of n companies have at the fixpoint, and if the derivations for 100 companies are about 320,000, what do you expect for 200?
Run it from the labs folder. The lab's semiNaive must get the 200-company chain down to 19,900 derivations.

code.title: NaiveRoundsDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.model.l09.demo /** * Naive Datalog evaluation of * controls(X, Y) :- owns(X, Y). * controls(X, Z) :- controls(X, Y), owns(Y, Z). * on ownership chains of growing length. Every round joins ALL facts found so far. */ fun main() { println("companies facts rounds derivations") for (n in listOf(50, 100, 200, 400)) { // C-1 owns C-2 owns C-3 ... owns C-n val owns = (1 until n).map { "C-$it" to "C-${it + 1}" }.toSet() val next = owns.groupBy({ it.first }, { it.second }) var controls: Set<Pair<String, String>> = owns // the first rule copies owns var derivations = owns.size.toLong() var rounds = 0 while (true) { rounds++ val derived = HashSet<Pair<String, String>>() for ((x, y) in controls) for (z in next[y].orEmpty()) { derived += x to z; derivations++ } val grown = controls + derived if (grown.size == controls.size) break // a round that adds nothing: the fixpoint controls = grown } println("%9d %6d %6d %,11d".format(n, controls.size, rounds, derivations)) } }

try.expect:
companies  facts    rounds  derivations
       50    1225      49       39,249
      100    4950      99      323,499
      200   19900     199    2,626,999
      400   79800     399   21,173,999

The facts grow as n(n-1)/2, one per pair of companies on the chain, and the rounds as n - 1, the longest path. The derivations grow eight times per doubling, about n³/3, because every round walks every fact found so far. At 200 companies naive evaluation does 132 derivations per fact it keeps. Semi-naive does exactly one.

refs.title: CodeQL: About the QL language (semantics based on Datalog)

sections.h: GraphQL is a query language for APIs, not a graph database
sections.html:
The third language in this lesson's title has "graph" in its name and isn't a database at all. GraphQL, which Facebook open-sourced in 2015, is a query language for an API. A mobile app or a web page sends one query that names the fields it wants, and the server answers with JSON in exactly that shape:

query {
  payments(merchant: "M-0042", last: 3) {
    id
    amountMinor
    account { iban customer { name } }
  }
}

The answer mirrors the query: a list of three payments, each with its account nested inside, each account with its customer's name. If two payments share an account, the account appears twice. GraphQL accepts that duplication on purpose, because the client gets something it can render without joining anything.

The server publishes a schema, typed much like a Kotlin interface: type Payment { id: ID!, amountMinor: Int!, account: Account }, where ! means not null. A client can ask only for fields the schema declares and follow only links the schema declares. There's no "every account within three hops" unless someone wrote a field for it, no recursion, and no arbitrary filtering. That's deliberate. Queries come from untrusted clients over the internet, so the server must be able to bound what any query costs, and production servers also cap query depth and complexity.

Behind the schema can be anything: PostgreSQL, DynamoDB, Neo4j, three REST services. So GraphQL doesn't replace a data model. It lives in the API layer, the territory of the Encoding, APIs and workflows track, and it decides how many calls reach the stores below. That number is where it goes wrong, which is the next section.

The specification moves slowly. The September 2025 edition is the first since October 2021. It added OneOf input objects (an input where exactly one field must be set) and schema coordinates, a standard way to name a field such as Payment.account. Streaming parts of a response with @defer and @stream is still a proposal.

try.title: Predict a response, and what the schema refuses
steps: The schema declares Query.payments(merchant, last), Payment { id, amountMinor, account }, Account { iban, customer } and Customer { name }. M-0042's three newest payments are pay-3 and pay-2 from account A-7 and pay-1 from account A-9.
Sketch the JSON for the query above. How many times does A-7's IBAN appear?
Does the server run { payments(merchant: "M-0042", last: 3) { account { payments { id } } } }? Decide before you read on.
try.expect:
{ "data": { "payments": [
    { "id": "pay-3", "amountMinor": ..., "account": { "iban": "<A-7's>", "customer": { "name": ... } } },
    { "id": "pay-2", "amountMinor": ..., "account": { "iban": "<A-7's>", "customer": { "name": ... } } },
    { "id": "pay-1", "amountMinor": ..., "account": { "iban": "<A-9's>", "customer": { "name": ... } } }
] } }

The response has the query's shape and nothing else, and A-7's IBAN appears twice, once under each of its payments. The second query is refused with a validation error before any resolver runs, because Account declares no payments field: a client can only follow links the schema offers. Add that field and the query becomes legal, and so does a query nested ten levels deep, which is why servers cap depth.

sections.h: One resolver per field makes N+1 calls, and batching makes one call per level
sections.html:
The server produces that answer by walking the query tree and calling a resolver, a function you write, for every field of every object. Query.payments runs once and returns 50 payments. Then Payment.account runs once per payment, each time asking the accounts service for one id: 50 calls. Then Account.customer runs once per account: 50 more. One query from the client became 101 calls behind the API.

This is the N+1 problem from the SQL track's lesson on JDBC, one query for the list and one per row, moved up into the API layer. Every call is a round trip. At about 2 ms a call, a fair figure for another service in the same data centre, 101 calls is about 200 ms before any real work, and the cost grows with the page size. GraphQL makes it worse in one way: the client chooses the query, so a new screen can add a nested field and multiply your call count without a deploy on your side.

The fix is batching, the pattern Facebook's DataLoader library made standard. A resolver doesn't fetch its one account at once. It hands the key to a loader and gets a promise back. When every resolver at that level has asked, the loader makes one call with all the distinct keys, accounts(ids), which is WHERE account_id = ANY(?) in SQL or one BatchGetItem in DynamoDB, and hands each resolver its record. 50 payments that use 12 accounts cost one call for 12 ids. Do the same for customers and the whole query costs 3 calls, one per level of the tree, however many payments the page shows. The loader also caches by key for one request, so an account that appears under 10 payments is fetched once.

Lesson 4's warning from DeBrie makes sense now. Single-table design pre-joins a screen so that one Query answers it, and a GraphQL server that resolves field by field throws that away unless its resolvers know about the single table. JVM frameworks put the batching where it belongs: Spring for GraphQL has @BatchMapping, and graphql-java has a DataLoader port, so you write one method that takes all the payments of a level and returns their accounts. The lab builds that by hand so you can count the calls.

try.title: Count the calls one query makes
steps: Read ResolverCallsDemo.kt. It resolves the payments query field by field, the naive way, for pages of 10, 50 and 200 payments, and every backend call sleeps 2 ms like a round trip to another service.
Predict the number of backend calls for each page size, and the time for 200 payments.
Run it from the labs folder. Then work out what a batched server would make for each page size.

code.title: ResolverCallsDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.model.l09.demo /** * One GraphQL query, resolved field by field: * { payments(merchant: "M-0042", last: N) { id amountMinor account { iban customer { name } } } } * Each backend call sleeps 2 ms, a round trip to another service or a database on the same network. */ private var calls = 0 private fun roundTrip() { calls++; Thread.sleep(2) } private data class Pay(val id: Int, val accountId: Int) private data class Acct(val id: Int, val customerId: Int) // the three resolvers a naive server runs: Query.payments, Payment.account, Account.customer private fun payments(n: Int): List<Pay> { roundTrip(); return (1..n).map { Pay(it, it % 12) } } private fun account(id: Int): Acct { roundTrip(); return Acct(id, id % 5) } private fun customer(id: Int): String { roundTrip(); return "Customer $id" } fun main() { payments(1).forEach { account(it.accountId) } // warm up the JIT, untimed println("payments backend calls time") for (n in listOf(10, 50, 200)) { calls = 0 val start = System.nanoTime() val response = payments(n).map { p -> val a = account(p.accountId) // once per payment Triple(p.id, a.id, customer(a.customerId)) // once per account } val ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000 check(response.size == n) println("%8d %13d %d ms".format(n, calls, ms)) } }

try.expect:
payments  backend calls  time
      10             21  55 ms
      50            101  248 ms
     200            401  991 ms

The calls are exact: 1 + N + N. The times are one run on a laptop and come out at about 2.5 ms a call, because Thread.sleep(2) sleeps at least 2 ms; yours will be close. A page of 200 payments spends a second waiting on round trips. Batched, each page size makes 3 calls, about 8 ms.

refs.title: DataLoader (GitHub): batching and caching for GraphQL resolvers

analogy: A triple store is a card index where every card has exactly three boxes: who, what, and to whom or what. A SPARQL query lays down a few cards with blanks and asks for every way to fill the blanks so the cards agree. Datalog adds rules pinned to the wall ("if a card says X owns Y and another says Y owns Z, write a card saying X controls Z"), and a clerk keeps applying them, looking only at the cards written since the last pass, until a pass writes nothing. GraphQL is the order slip a waiter takes: it lists exactly the dishes the table wants, and a kitchen that cooks each dish from scratch for each guest is slow however good the cooks are. The analogy breaks on scale and choice: a real clerk would notice the same card twice, while an engine only avoids repeated work if it's built to, and a real restaurant sets the menu, while a GraphQL client can order any combination the schema allows.
world: Know-your-customer checks ask a Datalog question every day: who ultimately controls this merchant, through any chain of holding companies? Company registers publish ownership as plain facts, and the answer is the controls rule, whether you write it as Datalog, a recursive CTE in Oracle or a SPARQL property path. Your GitHub repositories may already run Datalog: CodeQL code scanning evaluates QL queries over your Kotlin and Java. And if the merchant dashboard talks to your Quarkus services through a GraphQL gateway, count its backend calls per request before you blame the database: SmallRye GraphQL, the Quarkus implementation, batches when a @Source parameter is a List, and a field resolver written the other way turns one dashboard request into hundreds of REST calls to the payments service.
mistake: The most common mistake is writing a GraphQL resolver per field that calls its backend for one id, because that's how the schema reads and how every tutorial starts. It looks fine in development, where a page has 3 payments and every call takes a millisecond. In production the page has 50, each payment's account and customer is its own call, and one request becomes 101 round trips, more each time a client adds a nested field. The fix is a loader per type that collects the keys of one level and fetches them in one call with the distinct ids, plus a per-request cache, and a call counter in your integration tests so the number can't creep back up.

compare.title: Who controls M-0042: Datalog and a recursive CTE

a.label: Datalog
a.title: two rules and a query
a.html:
controls(X, Y) :- owns(X, Y).
controls(X, Z) :- controls(X, Y), owns(Y, Z).

?- controls(Who, "M-0042").

b.label: PostgreSQL WITH RECURSIVE
b.title: the same rules as SQL
b.html: WITH RECURSIVE controls(holder, company) AS ( SELECT holder, company FROM owns -- controls(X, Y) :- owns(X, Y). UNION SELECT c.holder, o.company -- controls(X, Z) :- FROM controls c -- controls(X, Y), JOIN owns o ON o.holder = c.company -- owns(Y, Z). ) SELECT holder FROM controls WHERE company = 'M-0042';

compare.note: Both say the same thing, and both evaluate semi-naively: the CTE's recursive term reads only the working table, and UNION drops rows already found, so a cycle of ownership ends too. Datalog is shorter because a rule is a join written with shared variables, and an engine is free to evaluate it from either end: given the constant in controls(Who, "M-0042"), it can rewrite the rules to start at M-0042 and walk upward (the magic-sets rewrite). The CTE as written derives every pair in the table and filters at the end, unless you start it from M-0042 yourself.

worked.title: Who ultimately controls M-0042, asked three ways

steps.say: Start from the facts, as triples. Two companies own C-7, and C-7 owns the merchant; C-1 sits one level higher.
steps.code:
ex:C-7  ex:owns  ex:M-0042 .
ex:C-2  ex:owns  ex:C-7 .
ex:C-9  ex:owns  ex:C-7 .
ex:C-1  ex:owns  ex:C-2 .

steps.say: SPARQL says "one or more owns hops" with a property path. The store follows ex:owns backward from M-0042 until it runs out.
Datalog says it with the two rules and a query. Semi-naive evaluation finds C-7 in round 0, C-2 and C-9 in round 1 and C-1 in round 2, then stops at the fixpoint in round 3, as the stepper showed.
steps.code:
controls(X, Y) :- owns(X, Y).
controls(X, Z) :- controls(X, Y), owns(Y, Z).
?- controls(C, "M-0042").
% C = "C-7" ; "C-2" ; "C-9" ; "C-1"

steps.say: GraphQL can't say it at all: there's no + and no recursion. The schema has to offer a field for it, and its resolver runs the recursion on the server, once, with one of the two forms above.

Count the calls. Exposing owners on merchants and companies and letting the client nest it four levels deep costs a call for the merchant, then one per company per level, and the client has to guess the depth. One field with a server-side recursion costs one call and needs no guess.
steps.code:
nested owners, 4 levels:  1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 6 calls here, more with every level and every owner
controllers field:        1 call, any depth

lab.title: A triple store, a semi-naive evaluator and a batched resolver
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. No Docker needed: this lab is plain Kotlin. 15 of the 17 tests fail with NotImplementedError; the two that pass check code you're given.

In TripleStore.kt, write match: for each stored triple, unify the pattern's subject, predicate and object with it, following the three rules in the KDoc. query is given and joins patterns with match. All six TripleStoreTest tests pass.

In Reachability.kt, naive is given. Write semiNaive: keep a delta, join only the delta with owns each round, count every pair you join as a derivation, and stop when a round adds nothing. The chain test expects 19,900 derivations on 200 companies, against naive's 2.6 million.

In Resolvers.kt, NaiveResolvers is given and makes 100 calls for 50 payments (one payment's account no longer exists). Write BatchedResolvers.resolve with one call per level. The tests check that the views are identical to the naive ones, that it makes 3 calls, and which ids each call asked for.
hints: A private helper unify(term, value, bindings): Bindings? that returns null on a mismatch keeps match short: run it for s, then p, then o, and keep the result if it isn't null.
Unify left to right with the growing map, and Pattern("?x", "owns", "?x") works for free: by the time you reach the object, ?x is already bound by the subject.
In semiNaive, test each derived fact against everything known so far, not against the delta, or a cycle of ownership never ends.
payments.mapTo(LinkedHashSet()) { it.accountId } collects the distinct ids in first-seen order. Skip the call when the set is empty: the empty-merchant test expects exactly 1 call.

drill.title: Rules, a path and a batch from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson. Write the two Datalog rules for controls over owns, the SPARQL query for every company that controls ex:M-0042 at any depth, and one sentence each on what semi-naive evaluation joins in a round and what a batched resolver sends per level.

answer.html:
controls(X, Y) :- owns(X, Y).
controls(X, Z) :- controls(X, Y), owns(Y, Z).

PREFIX ex: <https://example.test/pay#>
SELECT ?c WHERE { ?c ex:owns+ ex:M-0042 . }

Semi-naive: each round joins only the facts that were new in the previous round
(the delta) with owns, and stops when a round adds nothing (the fixpoint).
Batched resolver: one call per level of the query, carrying the distinct keys
that every resolver at that level asked for.

recap: RDF stores every fact as a triple (subject, predicate, object) with global IRI names, so datasets merge by putting them in one store. A SPARQL query is a set of triple patterns: a join of one three-column table with itself, and + property paths walk any depth.
In November 2026 RDF 1.2, with triple terms, is a W3C Candidate Recommendation and SPARQL 1.2 a Working Draft. RDF lives on in Wikidata, JSON-LD and Amazon Neptune.

Datalog: facts are rows, rules are views, and a rule may name itself. Evaluation runs to a fixpoint. Semi-naive evaluation joins only the previous round's new facts, 19,900 derivations instead of 2.6 million on a 200-company chain, and it's what PostgreSQL's working table does.
Datalog lives mostly as a tool: Datomic's queries, Soufflé's program analysis, GitHub's CodeQL and Google's Mangle.

GraphQL is an API query language over any backend: the response mirrors the query, clients can follow only declared fields, and there's no recursion. One resolver per field makes 1 + N + N calls; a loader that batches distinct keys makes one call per level.

explain.prompt: The merchant dashboard got slow the week the mobile team added account { customer { name } } to its payments query. A product manager says: "It's still one GraphQL query, so it can't be the API." Explain what changed, and how you'd fix it.
explain.answer: It's one query from the phone, but not one call behind the API. A GraphQL server runs a resolver for every field of every object. For a page of 50 payments, the payments resolver runs once, then the new account resolver runs once per payment and the customer resolver once per account, each a round trip to another service. So the page went from 1 call to 101, and at a couple of milliseconds a call that's about 200 ms more, growing with the page size. It's the N+1 problem from JDBC, one layer up. The fix is batching: a loader per type collects the account ids of all 50 payments and fetches them in one call with the distinct ids, then the same for customers, so the query costs 3 calls whatever the page size, with a per-request cache so a repeated account is fetched once. I'd also add a test that counts backend calls per query, so the next nested field can't quietly do it again.

deeper.html:
Datalog gets interesting when rules say "not". Say a holding company is idle if it controls no merchant:

company(X)  :- owns(X, _).
idle(X)     :- company(X), not controls_merchant(X).
controls_merchant(X) :- controls(X, M), merchant(M).

idle can be decided only once controls_merchant is complete, because a fact derived later could make a "not" false. So engines split the program into strata, layers that each depend only on finished layers below, and evaluate them in order. That's stratified negation, and a program whose recursion goes through a "not" has no strata and is rejected. SQL has a similar rule: PostgreSQL refuses a recursive reference inside a subquery such as NOT EXISTS, or on the nullable side of an outer join.

The second trick is the magic-sets rewrite from the compare block. A query like controls(Who, "M-0042") only needs the facts on paths that end at M-0042. The engine rewrites the rules so evaluation starts from the constant and walks backward, which turns "derive every pair, then filter" into "walk from the merchant". You'd do the same by hand in a recursive CTE by starting the anchor at M-0042.

RDF and property graphs differ most on edges with properties. A property graph puts since: 2024-03-01 on the OWNS relationship. Classic RDF had to turn the relationship into a node of its own, with extra triples for the subject, the object and the date. RDF 1.2's triple terms are the standard's answer: a triple can now be the object of another triple. Stonebraker and Pavlo treat RDF as a subset of property graphs, and that's the gap they mean.

For the bigger picture, chapter 3 of Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, walks through triple stores, Datalog and GraphQL as query languages for graph-shaped data, and explains why GraphQL deliberately leaves recursion out.
